name: Arc
license: AGPL-3.0 (Arc OSS); Arc Enterprise features ship in the same binary and are unlocked by a commercial licence key
summary: A young single-binary time-series database in Go that writes incoming data as Parquet files and queries them with DuckDB SQL.
intro: Arc is one Go binary with DuckDB compiled in. Clients send data over HTTP as InfluxDB line protocol (so Telegraf and other InfluxDB writers work unchanged), as columnar MessagePack, or through an MQTT subscription. Arc buffers rows in memory, with an optional write-ahead log, and flushes them about every 5 seconds as Parquet files laid out by database, measurement and hour, on local disk, S3 or an S3-compatible store, or Azure Blob. A background job merges each hour’s small files into one, then each day’s into one, dropping duplicate rows when the measurement has tags. Queries are SQL sent to an HTTP endpoint: Arc picks the partitions in the time range and hands them to DuckDB, returning JSON, MessagePack or Arrow. Since 26.09.1 it can also register its Parquet files as Apache Iceberg tables, so Spark or Trino read the same files.

The open-source build is AGPL-3.0. Basekick Labs sells Arc Enterprise, which uses a licence key to switch on clustering with writer, reader and compactor roles and automatic failover, role-based access control with SSO, hot/cold tiering, scheduled continuous queries and retention, and query quotas. On 2026-10-06 it was listed at $5,000 a year for up to 8 cores, $15,000 for up to 32 cores and $40,000 for up to 128 cores, billed annually. Arc Cloud launched in April 2026 with plans from $50 a month; Basekick’s managed page now offers Arc Enterprise Managed on dedicated servers, priced per agreement. The first commit was on October 7, 2025, so Arc is a year old, with 16 releases on GitHub so far.
strengths: Data stays in open Parquet files on your own disk or bucket, readable by DuckDB, Spark or any Parquet tool, and since 26.09.1 also as Iceberg tables
Drop-in ingestion for InfluxDB setups: line protocol endpoints compatible with InfluxDB 1.x and 2.x, a Telegraf output plugin, and `tsm2arc` to import InfluxDB’s files from disk
One binary with no external services: a laptop, an edge box or a Kubernetes pod via the Helm chart, with an optional FIPS 140-3 build
Full DuckDB SQL (joins, window functions, CTEs) over current and historical data in one query
AGPL-3.0 from the first public release, with the licence and the commercial option stated up front
limits: Young: first commit October 2025, rewritten from Python to Go within two months, and recent patch releases still fix clustering and data-loss bugs, such as a shutdown path in 26.09.2 that could drop acknowledged writes during a storage outage

Open core: clustering, failover, RBAC, tiering, and scheduled retention and continuous queries need Arc Enterprise; in the open build, retention policies and continuous queries run only when you trigger them
AGPL-3.0: changes you distribute or offer as a network service must be published, which some companies’ policies rule out, so they need the commercial licence

Headline numbers are Basekick’s own: 34 million records a second was measured on a MacBook Pro, and its first ClickBench submission in October 2025 was rerun after ClickBench maintainers flagged cache flushing, leaving cold runs about three times slower
The engine may change: Basekick plans ArcX, a proprietary query engine meant to replace DuckDB in Arc

snippet.title: Write line protocol, then query it with SQL
source: # two readings in InfluxDB line protocol (nanosecond timestamps)
# buffered rows are flushed to Parquet every 5 s by default; then query with DuckDB SQL
{"sql": "SELECT well, date_trunc('hour', time) AS hour, max(psi) AS peak_psi FROM pressure WHERE time > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY GROUP BY well, hour ORDER BY hour"}

notes: When an Enterprise key expires (after a 14-day grace period), Arc falls back to OSS behaviour: ingestion, queries and compaction keep working, while clustering, RBAC and tiering switch off.
Enterprise licences are tied to machine fingerprints and validated locally, so air-gapped sites can activate them offline.

story: Ignacio Van Droogenbroeck, a former InfluxData employee, started in November 2022 with a side project: an API to deploy hosted time-series databases on several clouds. By 2023 he ran it full time, hosting InfluxDB, TimescaleDB and QuestDB for customers, mostly in Latin America, and wanted a database of his own. A first attempt, Wavestream, managed about 20,000 writes a second and ended in 2024.

He started again with Historian, a tiered-storage add-on that copied InfluxDB 1.x and 2.x data into Parquet files on S3 and used DuckDB to query them. Sold to InfluxDB Enterprise customers with scaling problems, it gradually grew into a database, which Basekick Labs, based in Costa Rica, published as Arc in October 2025 under AGPL-3.0.

The first version was written in Python to test demand quickly. After memory leaks in its multi-worker design, Basekick rewrote all 18,280 lines in Go for release 25.12.1, shipped at the end of November 2025. Enterprise clustering, a managed cloud and Iceberg tables followed in 2026.

choices.choice: Plain Parquet files instead of a private storage format
choices.why: Historian had already shown that time-series data could live as Parquet on S3, and open files mean customers can query or leave with their data without Arc.
Rather than write a SQL engine, Basekick built on DuckDB, which had started as Historian’s way to run SQL over Parquet files.
Van Droogenbroeck had watched Redis, Elastic and MinIO change licences after cloud providers resold their work, and wanted the rules and the commercial licence stated before anyone depended on Arc.
DuckDB’s memory allocator keeps memory after each job, so long-running compaction bloated the server; a child process returns everything to the OS when it exits and can’t crash the API.

timeline.text: Side project to host time-series databases begins in November
First prototype, Wavestream, is abandoned; work on Historian begins
Arc published under AGPL-3.0 in October; Go rewrite ships in November
Arc Cloud in April; quarterly releases from June; Iceberg in September
